Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drift off into a world of my own
I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

vignette: Samir was twelve when the plaster cracked down the hallway, but it was his father's voice that carved itself into him first. The man who once taught him to throw a baseball became a stranger who shouted, slammed doors, and dragged a chair across the floor until the wood splintered. When Samir tried to piece together those years, he found himself staring at hyper-detailed snapshots in his mind-the exact scuff marks on the baseboard, the way the streetlamp caught the dust in the air-while the hours before and after remained completely erased. He knew that if he forced himself to deliberately recall the sequence of events, the images would simply dissolve, leaving only a heavy, hollow pressure in his chest. As an adult, that wiring followed him to the framing floor. The moment a city inspector's cruiser pulled into the gravel lot or a project manager raised his voice over the concrete mixer, Samir's breath would catch and his shoulders would lock against his ribs, the physical readiness for violence kicking in before his mind could even process the request. When those authority figures approached with sudden expectations, they did not just bring physical alarm; they unlocked the exact, hyper-detailed snapshots of the hallway nights, while leaving the surrounding hours completely dark. Samir had come to believe that his body was the first to sound the alert, so he quickly learned to sidestep any discussion about deadlines, assuming that when projects dragged on longer than expected, disaster was already loading in the wings. Those sudden intrusions of memory did not just haunt him; they dictated his next moves. When a photograph of a shattered doorframe would surface without warning, Samir would immediately scan the crew for tight jaws or shifting stances, convinced that violence was only a breath away. He would retreat into a mental fog, replaying old clips of how he used to be before the violence took hold, because dwelling on a safer past felt less dangerous than facing the present. And because the memories kept surfacing unbidden, he began to interpret any future planning as a trap, flinching whenever anyone asked him to commit to a schedule months out. What frightened him most was that the past kept bleeding into the present, turning every neutral timeline into a countdown. On the scaffolding, the constant scanning of faces and the dread of delayed permits turned his body into a warning system. When a forklift backed up slower than expected, the physical tension in his chest would surge, and the only thing that stopped him from shouting or fleeing was the habit of slipping into a private fantasy where he was no longer on a job site. The physical alarm pulled sharper, unbidden images of the splintered chair and cracked plaster to the front of his mind, making the event feel like it was happening now rather than years ago. He would retreat into those daydreams, and the act of escaping only hardened the boundaries around his trauma; the longer he drifted away, the more impossible it became to pull the actual footage of the event from his mind, leaving only the raw snapshots intact. Over the years, the habit of avoidance and the refuge of internal daydreams did exactly what he feared they would. By refusing to engage in disagreements and retreating into his own head, he slowly rewired his environment; every time he avoided a discussion, the unresolved tension festered until even a neutral question from a coworker triggered the same old alarm. His refusal to engage meant that even minor requests from supervisors now landed like personal attacks, and the distance he built into his own head only kept his nervous system permanently dialed up. He stopped looking forward to anything, convinced that planning only painted a target on his back. Samir, now forty-one, finally walked into a clinic after a routine inspection triggered a full-body tremor that lasted nearly an hour, leaving him unable to climb back onto the framing line. He had come to believe that his body was betraying him, that the constant scanning and the mental escapes were failing him, and that the only way to keep his job-and his life-intact was to finally sit down with someone who understood how fear works. He hoped, more than anything, to learn how to stand in a room without his heart racing, and to figure out why the future kept feeling like a threat.
